title: My experience building a game with AI (I'm a Blue Collar Worker)
author: Ancient-Elevator5158
selftext:
TLDR  
How its going: I'm having fun  
What I'm making: A Multiplayer Survival Crafting RPG  
Am i going to monetize it: No just for me and some friends to screw around with  
Is it a waste of time: Oh yeah, but im having fun  
Do I have anything Playable: I have a lot of pieces of a game that i can play individually so far, and am starting to bring things together to build on them.

First off, this game is never going to be released. I’m not trying to sell it or make the next big thing. I just have an idea for a game I want to play with my friends, and I’m having fun making it.

I’m using AI to help me build it. I’m also using a version configured so my project conversations and data aren’t used to train the model.

The way I use it is pretty much: I come up with an idea, talk it through with the AI, and we break it down into things that actually need to be made. It helps me figure out how systems should work together, look through project files, work on code, troubleshoot problems, and run checks.

I still make the decisions about what I want in the game. Sometimes the AI comes up with something useful, and sometimes I have to tell it that’s not what I meant and go over it again. It also makes mistakes and can act like something is working just because a test passed, so I have to check what actually happened.

I also have a project hub called **Compass** that we built to keep track of everything. It keeps the game’s systems, decisions, tasks, dependencies, assets, and testing notes in one place. It saves where we left off so I don’t have to explain the whole game again every time I start a new chat.

One of the things I’m trying to keep track of is the difference between an idea, something I’ve decided I want, something we’ve built, and something that’s actually been tested working with the rest of the game. Because apparently having a ton of documents about a game doesn’t mean you have a game. Who knew?

**For assets**, I’m using existing ones that allow the kind of AI use I’m doing, and repurposing them as I need them. I’m not trying to generate every single thing from scratch. There are already a million renditions of trees in the world, so why waste water generating another pine tree when I can use one that already exists?

I’m also making the game in a bunch of smaller pieces, and whenever possible, I like to outsource the work to my friends. By outsource, I mean I make them do it for free and call it helping.

For example, instead of building every region myself, I made a map editor, gave it to my friends, and had each of them build and develop a region. So they get to help create the world we’re going to play in, and I get free labor. Everybody wins. Mostly me.

That’s kind of how I’m approaching a lot of the game: make a smaller tool or system, get it working, and then use it to build part of the bigger game. AI helps me work through and build those tools, and my friends help me fill the world with stuff.

Right now I have a bunch of individual pieces and experiments. The goal is to start connecting them into something my friends and I can actually play together, then keep building from there.

Is making a multiplayer survival crafting RPG for a handful of people an absolutely ridiculous amount of work? Probably.

Am I having fun? Yep.

comments.author: Furyan9x
comments.body:
Fellow blue collar AI game dev here!! 

Im also having a great time and do not care one bit about the cost or the outcome. The journey so far has been very fulfilling and seeing my ideas come to life through the AIs intelligence and know-how is a high I haven't experienced in a long long time.

comments.author: Fancy-Proof-9449
comments.body:
"Having a ton of documents about a game doesn't mean you have a game" is the most honest line I've read here this week.

The thing you said about it acting like something works because a test passed, I fixed that for myself by changing what "done" means. Done isn't "the test passed", it's built, tested, and I saw it working on my phone. If I didn't see it, it's not done, however confident the message sounds.

The idea / decided / built / tested split is smart. I'd add one thing to it: write down why you decided something, on the same line. A lot of the times I thought the AI was ignoring me, it just didn't know I'd already decided that two chats ago, or why.

And the map editor for your friends is great. Making a tool and letting other people fill the world is how a lot of real studios work too.
